spec.name: BeishaheBridge
spec.coordinateSystem: Local glTF axes: X transverse to bridge, Y up, Z along bridge from its north end toward its south end; origin at bridge center, sleeper top Y=0. X and Z are not geographic east and south until a placement transform is applied.
spec.reconstructionScope: Independent intact bridge candidate. Its 280 m length follows the present-day crossing/floodplain scale, not a proven 1938 bridge length. Fourteen 20 m spans, all member sections, the transverse timber deck and support layout, pier dimensions, deck elevation, damp staining, weathering and colors are authored design; none establishes the appearance or water level in March 1938. The 44 m compressed FirstLevel1218 blockout and legacy pontoon bridge are not replaced.

historicalReferences.image: JACAR C11111424100 appendix photo 12, 567 km bridge north of Tengxian
historicalReferences.supports: Nearby 1938 low pony truss silhouette, straight upper chord, inclined end posts, open above the track. Not identified as Beishahe itself.
Nearby short steel trusses, masonry support and demolition appearance. Not the Beishahe bridge.
User research archive; exact 1938 Beishahe bridge photograph still unconfirmed.

historicalReferences.supports: Retained as an earlier geometric diagnostic only. Its modern red-brown finish has been rejected as a color source; it does not establish the historical Beishahe pattern, member sections, coating color or condition.
1937 route description lists 1.435 m gauge and nominal 10 m, 41 kg/m rails for Tianjin-Xuzhou. Exact joint positions, rail section and bridge-specific fittings are not established.
1913 reference shows square-headed screw spikes with circular flanges for Prussian and Alsace-Lorraine railway track; an engineering analogy, not a photograph or specification of Beishahe.
1908 Minnesota road bridge: paired riveted members and gusset/floor-beam connections as an engineering analogy. Not a Chinese railway bridge, not evidence of Beishahe-specific details.

HAER WV-64 photograph 14 records the riveted upper chord and gusset of a 1936 American road bridge; the photograph is dated 1997 by Wikimedia Commons. This is a construction analogy, not a railway bridge or evidence of Beishahe-specific dimensions and rivet layout.

A 2005 covered-bridge manual describes deck planks spiked to supporting stringers, commonly two at each connection. This general highway-bridge analogy does not establish the original Beishahe deck, nail type, size, placement or structural adequacy; the model's short fasteners are not claimed to meet the manual's vehicular-deck recommendations.

1941 Jinpu railway bridge at an unknown location: outside longitudinal timbers and a visible timber joint provide an engineering reference. Neither the dimensions nor their presence at Beishahe is established.

US Bureau of Labor Statistics Bulletin 188, March 1916, pp.77-78, reproduces British railway-engineer evidence describing black coal-tar protective paint on railway river bridges. This is a foreign period process analogy only; it does not establish the coating type, color or condition of the Beishahe bridge.

mapMeasurement.centerWgs84Role: Original map-query center, retained for compatibility; not the computed center of either mapped bridge.

illustrativeModernPlacement.originDefinition: Arithmetic mean of the four mapped endpoints; midway between two modern bridge axes, not the center of either individual bridge.
illustrativeModernPlacement.method: WGS84 ellipsoid ECEF projected to an east-north-up tangent plane at origin; average paired north endpoints and south endpoints before computing horizontal bearing.
illustrativeModernPlacement.conversion: east=0.760081535*x+0.649827716*z; north=0.649827716*x-0.760081535*z; up=y (all metres relative to the chosen origin and bridge-local vertical datum).
illustrativeModernPlacement.verticalDatum: Relative model Y=0 is sleeper top. Absolute elevation, bridge-deck height, and WGS84 ellipsoidal height are unknown.
illustrativeModernPlacement.limitations: Illustrative alignment to the midpoint between the modern twin bridges only; 280 m model support-axis length is not scaled to fit the 280.415 m mean axis. No 1938 bridge location, orientation, elevation, or original size is established.

modernWaterwaySketch.limitations: Coarse straight interpolation of adjacent modern OSM river-centerline nodes, not a surveyed channel or bank; angle and crossing are rough illustration only, with unquantified generalization error. They do not establish 1938 river alignment or conditions.

mapMeasurement.imagery: Esri World Imagery; OSM bridge endpoints checked against visible modern bridge ends
mapMeasurement.uncertainty: Modern mapped crossing includes floodplain. Water-channel estimate is image interpretation, approximately +/-5 to 10 m. Neither establishes the 1938 bank position or original bridge length. Model is deliberately rounded to 280 m.

masonryMaintenance.interpretation: Unique authored old mineral-wash remnants, partial gray rebrushing, runoff and worn stone corners. These do not establish the original bridge's maintenance history, coating type, color or water level.

materialInterpretation.trussBracing: Nine panels and three central counterbraced bays are authored geometry decisions. The 1934 printed Xianning image and nearby 1938 JACAR bridges support only the broad low, open-top silhouette; exact sections, nodes, fasteners and face assignments are not established for Beishahe. The modern photograph is retained only as an earlier geometric diagnostic.
materialInterpretation.trussMainMembers: The 0.21 m in-plane main-member depth is an authored apparent-width match to isolated near-side faces in the modern Xianning photograph, checked with full 3D projection. It is not a measured historical section; the 0.09 m end-post setback preserves the structural span gap. Paired-channel transverse width, vertical members, chords, counterbars and material images remain unchanged.
materialInterpretation.trussConnections: Extended upper gusset plates, packers and domed rivet groups are a design analogy to the 1936 Easley road bridge; their exact form and dimensions are not established for Beishahe. The rivet heads are modeled without shanks or holes.
materialInterpretation.trussFinish: Dark charcoal-gray aged protective coating is an imagegen design study selected per user direction. The modern red-brown finish is no longer used. A 1916 foreign railway-bridge coating record is a period process analogy only; the original Beishahe coating type, color and wear remain unverified. The rail body keeps its separate neutral steel texture.
materialInterpretation.pierDamp: Irregular brown-gray and muted olive staining that fades into the dry pier is a creative weathering choice, not evidence of the 1938 waterline or site condition.
materialInterpretation.pierJointShade: Continuous darkening over each real stone bevel and recessed side is an authored occlusion-style visual treatment. It is not a measured mortar color, a lightmap, or evidence of the 1938 bridge's masonry.
materialInterpretation.pierMasonry: Varying stone lengths and staggered joints are an authored visual analogy to the AI construction study, not a measured masonry bond of the 1938 Beishahe bridge.
materialInterpretation.pierStoneEdges: Unequal corner bevels and their occlusion-style shading are authored visual analogies to the rough stone edges in the AI construction study, not measured original stone damage.
materialInterpretation.masonryMaintenance: Selected stone corners and cap edges are worn back, with unique per-support old mineral-wash remnants, partial gray rebrushing and downward runoff. Thin closed coating meshes share an authored mineral-wash PBR set derived from the retained V5 imagegen study; no original repair campaign, coating type or maintenance date is established.
materialInterpretation.pierStoneSurface: The retained V2 imagegen stone source and a 20 percent generated weathering blend provide broad hewn marks. Fine surface occlusion is restrained with a 0.15 bake factor, preserving the existing albedo, normal maps and geometric joint shading. The PBR calibration and inferred relief are authored material choices, not measurements of the 1938 bridge.
materialInterpretation.bearings: Fixed cast shoes, expansion rollers, baseplates, four-corner anchors and abutment support extensions are authored construction interpretations. The AI detail guides the fixed shoe's visible form; no original Beishahe bearing type, anchor dimensions or structural rating is established. Anchor shafts intentionally overlap undrilled plate and stone; threads and holes are not modeled.
materialInterpretation.pierCap: Four individually jointed capstones with a solid inset base are an authored interpretation of an AI detail study, not evidence for the historic Beishahe pier cap.
materialInterpretation.deckPlanks: In response to the user's request for a complete deck, transverse planks were selected from the generated design study; presence and details are not established by a confirmed 1938 Beishahe bridge photograph.
materialInterpretation.deckFasteners: Paired cylinder fasteners at the two inner bearers are an authored analogy to general timber-deck connections, not a documented 1938 Beishahe detail. The simplified 71 mm solids overlap undrilled wood, have no threads or distinct head, and are not a structural design or a claim of compliance with vehicular-deck guidance.
materialInterpretation.jointTransitions: Rail and wooden deck splice details are authored to maintain a usable crossing; their exact construction is not established by a confirmed 1938 Beishahe bridge photograph.
materialInterpretation.railJoints: The 1937 route record gives nominal 10 m rails, while joint positions at midspan and supports, the 6 mm gaps, section dimensions and hardware are authored design assumptions. Represented through-bolt shafts overlap solid undrilled rail webs and plates.
materialInterpretation.railFasteners: Square-head screw-spike shape, 120 mm sleeper embed, two outside and one inside, and outside hook plates are authored interpretations of early German railway references, not established for the 1938 Beishahe bridge. Solid spike shafts intentionally overlap undrilled sleeper and tie-plate geometry; holes and threads are not modeled.
materialInterpretation.guardTimbers: Two low outer longitudinal timbers are an authored interpretation of a 1941 Jinpu railway bridge photograph at an unknown location; their use and dimensions at Beishahe are unconfirmed.
